title: DERMA-GUARD: Evidence-Aware Specialist Consensus with Risk-Controlled Evidence Acquisition and Deferral for Multimodal Dermatology
name: RACHIT AGARWAL
keywords: multimodal dermatology, evidential deep learning, Dempster-Shafer fusion, learned evidence gating, conformal prediction, Learn-then-Test, selective prediction, evidence acquisition, clinical decision support

abstract: Artificial intelligence for skin-lesion diagnosis has reached impressive accuracy on curated image collections, and smartphone apps that photograph a mole and return a diagnosis are already in public use. Almost all of these systems share a dangerous habit: they always answer. A blurred photograph, missing patient history, or an image and history that point to different diagnoses still produce a confident label, and the confidence shown is rarely calibrated. In dermatology the costliest error is a cancer that is confidently called harmless, so a system that cannot say "I am not sure" is not safe to deploy.

This project presents DERMA-GUARD, a decision-support system that behaves more like a careful clinician. Six specialist models examine a lesion: evidential neural heads for the clinical photograph, the dermoscopic image and the patient details, the image model of our earlier prototype, a vote of the most similar past cases, and a class-balanced classifier over learned embeddings. A Devil's Advocate component profiles every specialist on every case (input quality, learned reliability, uncertainty, track record for the suspected diagnosis, agreement, consistency, missing inputs and out-of-distribution distance), and a learned evidence gate decides how much each opinion should count. Seven combination rules were compared under cross-fitting and the rule was chosen on validation data only. A calibrated, cost-aware policy then chooses among four outcomes: a high-confidence answer, a clearly marked low-confidence answer that a doctor confirms, a request for more evidence (a dermoscopic image, missing details or a better photograph), or deferral when the evidence contradicts itself. The missed-cancer rate of high-confidence answers is certified with Learn-then-Test, and the system is wrapped in a care platform with a patient app, a doctor review queue, explanations of every decision, messaging, follow-ups and an audit log.

On 787 held-out lesions of the MILK10k dataset, in which every lesion has both a clinical and a dermoscopic image, DERMA-GUARD answers 89.1% of patients; 57.1% receive a high-confidence answer that is 77.1% accurate across eleven diagnoses and misses 3.1% of cancers. The learned fusion raises photograph-only macro-F1 from 0.286 to 0.377. A learned rejector misses significantly more cancers at the same coverage (4.9%), while plain confidence thresholding is close (3.8%); across four fusion back-ends the policy's miss rate stays between 3.0% and 3.5% while thresholding swings between 3.5% and 9.3%. Controlled image damage shows that evidential uncertainty alone does not notice blur, darkness, noise or occlusion; explicit quality checks and requests for missing details remove every confident answer on damaged input. External tests on PAD-UFES-20 and Derm7pt, without retraining, show the safety decision transferring while fine-grained diagnosis does not. An audit of our earlier prototype found that its reported 84-90% accuracies came from an evaluation that adjusted predictions toward preset targets; re-scored honestly its models reach 57-75% on unseen patients. The project therefore contributes not only a working system but a fully reproducible, honestly evaluated one.
